title: Delegated Claims Patterns and Audit Stream Design
content:
Purpose

Working notes for a delegated-permissions model that complements RBAC v2 and defines an audit-friendly event schema for SIEM ingestion and evidence automation. This is a design + rollout sketch rather than a finalized spec. Main goals: enable short-lived delegation, preserve auditable chains (who delegated what to whom), and produce SIEM-friendly event records that can support compliance evidence exports.

Context / motivation
- RBAC v2 gives us role/attribute mapping and fine-grained entitlements. For many products we need temporary delegation (service-to-service acts-on-behalf-of, customer support escalation, cross-team ops).
- Current audit logs lack structured delegation metadata; downstream SIEM rules struggle to answer questions like: who granted the permission, what was the scope, and was the delegation later revoked?
- Evidence automation requires compact, linkable proofs (attestation references) rather than blobs.

Scope
- Focus on delegation patterns (explicit claim, token-bound, attestation chain).
- Define a canonical audit event envelope for both realtime SIEM ingest and offline evidence export.
- Migration constraints: compatible with RBAC v1 logs; non-blocking rollout.

High-level pattern options (trade-offs)
1) Delegated Claim Tokens (preferred)
   - A short-lived JWT-like claim object (opaque to caller if necessary) with fields: delegator_id, delegatee_id, scope, expiry, edge_proof_ref.
   - Issued by an authorization service (Authz) after evaluating policy; stored once in a durable store for evidence retrieval.
   - Pros: compact, self-contained for runtime enforcement, easy to include in audit traces.
   - Cons: requires token issuance path and storage + lifecycle ops.

2) Attestation Chain References
   - Instead of embedding full claim, runtime logs include a reference id that maps to a stored attestation chain: [grant event -> approvals -> revocations]. SIEM pulls full chain on-demand via CI/CD or scheduled enrichment jobs.
   - Pros: minimal token surface; helpful for long post-hoc investigation.
   - Cons: SIEM queries for enrichment increase complexity/cost; real-time alerting suffers unless enrichment done pre-ingest.

3) Ephemeral Role Borrowing (no token)
   - Borrow a role for X minutes via internal flow; runtime logs capture both original actor and effective role with a borrow_id. Enforcement checks borrow_id validity at call time.
   - Pros: simple UX.
   - Cons: less explicit about who granted permission unless borrow metadata captured.

Canonical Audit Event envelope (core fields)
- event_id: uuid
- timestamp: iso8601
- event_type: string (auth.grant | auth.use | auth.revoke | entitlement.change)
- actor: { id: string, type: user|service }
- effective_principal: { id: string, type: user|service }   // who executed under
- resource: string (resource id / route / model endpoint)
- action: string (read|write|generate|admin)
- delegation: string | null  // either claim_id or attestation_ref
- decision: allowed|denied|fallback
- policy_snapshot_ref: string | null // reference to policy version used
- evidence_refs: [list of short ids] // links to stored artifacts (approval emails, audit snapshots)

Example event (single line for ingestion)
{
  "event_id": "e7a9b2d4-9f3a-4a2f-8cde-1a2b3c4d5e6f",
  "timestamp": "2025-01-12T18:34:21Z",
  "event_type": "auth.use",
  "actor": "svc:ingest-pipeline",
  "effective_principal": "user:alice@redwood.ai",
  "resource": "/models/llama-2/generate",
  "action": "generate",
  "delegation": "claim:dc-113c",
  "decision": "allowed",
  "policy_snapshot_ref": "policy:v2025-01-10",
  "evidence_refs": ["att:att-781"]
}

Notes about the envelope:
- Keep fields flat for SIEM mapping (avoid nested objects where possible). If nested objects are needed, they should be stringified JSON in a single field for easy ingestion.
- event_type becomes a primary dimension in detection rules.
- delegation should point to a small stable id rather than inline blobs where possible.

Evidence automation model
- On grant: create attestation document (structured JSON) that contains: grantor, grantee, scope, time, reason, approvals (list of approvers), policy_version, expiry. Persist attestation to a durable store (S3-like) and index a short id (att-xxx) in the auth DB.
- On use: include attestation id in audit event (delegation field). If attestation expired/absent, log as unauthenticated/denied but capture all context.
- On revoke: write revocation record that references original attestation id; mark attestation as revoked and emit an entitlement.change event.
- Evidence export: support a query API to snapshot all events + attestation docs for a given time window/actor/tenant, packaged as a compliance bundle (minimal artifacts: events.csv, attestations.jsonl, policy_snapshots.tar.gz).

Sampling & retention strategy for SIEM ingest
- Full ingest for: auth.grant, auth.revoke, entitlement.change (these are lower volume).
- Sampled ingest for high-volume auth.use events (e.g., 0.5% for model.generate in hosted infra) with deterministic sampling keyed on tenant_id so you can reconstruct per-tenant samples consistently.
- Retention: SIEM raw index keep 90 days; compliance bundles retained per customer for configurable retention (default 1 year) in cold storage.

Migration and rollout plan (phased)
Phase 0 — pilot (1–2 months)
- Implement claim_id generation in Authz service and attach to new grants in a single internal workspace. Emit auth.grant and auth.use events with delegation set.
- Add lightweight attestation store (S3) + index. Wire minimal SIEM parsers to accept new envelope.

Phase 1 — opt-in tenants (3 months)
- Expose delegated-claim flows to Support + SRE via controlled UI and CLI (feature flagged). Start collecting usage signals and false-positive rates.
- Run daily enrichment job that stitches recent events with attestations for SIEM dashboards.

Phase 2 — platform-wide (3–6 months)
- Default integration for new RBAC v2 grants; when creating role mappings, system creates attestations for manual role bindings.
- Turn on deterministic sampling for high-volume events and route full grant/revoke events to SIEM.

Phase 3 — evidence automation & exports (6–12 months)
- Build compliance bundle generator and access controls for customers / internal auditors. Add APIs to revoke attestations and run snapshot exports.

Compatibility considerations
- RBAC v1 logs: provide a transformation layer that maps old fields into new envelope (best-effort). Use the grant_id=legacy-<id> pattern for traceability.
- Downstream dashboards: maintain a compatibility view for Kibana/Looker until consumers transition.

Operational concerns
- Storage costs for attestations: aim to store denormalized small JSONs; compress & gzip on write. Consider TTLs and encrypted buckets (customer keys for private deployments).
- Latency: claim issuance should be sub-50ms in the common path. If issuance causes latency spikes, fall back to issuing a reference and performing async issuance.
- Availability: attestation store must be highly available for evidence retrieval paths but can be served from cold storage for older records.

Open questions / risks
- Who is authorized to create an attestation? Do we allow service accounts to act as grantors? (UX vs safety)
- How do we represent compound delegations (A delegates to B who delegates to C) without creating excessively long chains in event logs?
- Policy snapshoting: what granularity for policy snapshots (per-change vs daily)?

Next steps / action items
- (Aisha) Draft minimal claim token format and edge-proof fields — target 2025-02-03.
- (Marco) Prototype attestation storage schema and index surface — target 2025-02-10.
- (Claire) Wire SIEM parsers and build sample dashboards for grant/revoke — target 2025-02-17.
- Create JIRA epic (SEC-CLAIM-PATTERNS) to track work and link to this doc.

Appendix: compact attestation example (human readable)
{
  "attestation_id": "att-781",
  "issued_at": "2025-01-12T18:10:05Z",
  "grantor": "user:bob@redwood.ai",
  "grantee": "svc:ingest-pipeline",
  "scope": ["/models/llama-2:generate"],
  "expiry": "2025-01-12T20:10:05Z",
  "approvals": ["user:sec-approver"],
  "policy_version": "policy:v2025-01-10"
}

Notes to reviewers: this doc is intentionally operational (lots of TODOs). Looking for feedback on the trade-offs and whether to favor inline small claim objects vs reference-only attestation ids for runtime logs. Also need recommendations on sampling rates for hosted high-volume endpoints.

Older revisions / context links
